newsitem.title: FRANCE: Security alert casts cloud over French Christmas.
newsitem.headline: Security alert casts cloud over French Christmas.

text.p: When Santa Claus goes to work in bomb-wary Paris, he must pass by armed soldiers and show his bag packed with his red costume and white beard to guards equipped with metal detectors.
Eventually, he reaches the department store's toys section, sits in his armchair and waits for kids to jump on his lap.

Christmas in France this year will be darkened by the "Vigipirate" security plan, reintroduced after a bomb in a Paris rush-hour train by suspected Algerian Islamic guerrillas killed four people and triggered fears of new attacks.

Jean-Christophe, the young actor who is Santa for the Galeries Lafayette store, works every day from half past nine until seven at night but never complains. "The happiness I see in the children's eyes has no price," he said.
The street outside is crowded with families who stop under the bright lights to admire the dancing puppets in shop windows.
But if they turned around, they would spot a dozen police vans parked behind the ornate Paris Opera.
"It's a bit odd to see policemen everywhere when you're looking for Christmas presents," said Marie, a young woman carrying bags full of innocent-looking parcels.

In a high-profile show of strength designed to reassure and deter, soldiers and police have tightened surveillance around the capital's railway stations and tourist sites such as the Eiffel Tower and major department stores.

According to the police unions, some 80 per cent of France's 89,000 uniformed police officers are participating in the Vigipirate plan including some 50 units of riot police comprising some 95 men each.
Paramilitary gendarmes and members of the regular armed forces have also been called up.
Travellers on the Paris Metro underground railway are bombarded with regular annoucements telling them to watch out for suspicious packages. Delays are frequent due to bomb alerts.

"We've been through that before," said Pierre, a commuter, remembering last year's bombings claimed by the radical Algerian Armed Islamic Group (GIA) that killed eight people and wounded more than 160 others.
"What's really a nuisance is that you can't throw anything away," he said, pointing to the sealed off rubbish bins with empty bottles and cigarette packs piled on their lids.
"People understand what we're here for," said a soldier patrolling the Auber underground station, near several large stores. "Some grumble but most of the time, they smile at us."
Outside Paris, as well, frequent police checks have not put a damper on holiday shopping.

"My turnover will be roughly the same as last year," said Sylvie, who owns a jewellery shop in the northern city of Lille. "People come to town without any fear. The bomb was in Paris. Here, people don't feel too concerned."
Fine restaurants are preparing for clients who will pay as much as 1,500 francs (around $300) for a meal on Christmas eve.

"The staff will be more careful than usual," said chef Andre Daguin, owner of a combined restaurant and hotel in Auch, southwestern France. "We have to make sure that no luggage gets left behind. We also take a close look at the parcels we receive, especially if they are addressed to clients."
At the end of the day, Santa Claus is exhausted.
"My arms and legs hurt," said Jean-Christophe, lifting up a blonde little girl with bright blue eyes. "But it's okay, it's nice and warm in here."
Outside, the soldiers are getting cold.
